title: Field methods for above and belowground biomass estimation in plantation forests
author: Huynh, Lee, et al.

steps.title: Prepare sample trees for felling
steps.instruction: Carry out all actions required before felling each selected tree.

substeps.instruction: Assign a unique tree identification number (ID) to each sample tree.
Clear the area around the selected tree of existing vegetation to avoid contamination; this can be done with an excavator or chainsaw.
Mark each tree at 50 cm height from the ground; this mark defines the boundary between above‑ground and below‑ground components and facilitates felling and stump handling.

steps.title: Record tree dimensions
steps.instruction: Measure and record the size parameters needed for biomass calculations.

substeps.instruction: Measure diameter at breast height (DBH) in centimeters and record it for each tree.
Measure crown diameter (CD) in meters in two perpendicular directions (along the planting row and across the planting row).
Calculate the average crown diameter and canopy area (CA, m²) using the equation CA = π·CD²/4.

steps.title: Set up weighing equipment
steps.instruction: Prepare all scales and balances required for weighing tree components in the field and laboratory.

substeps.instruction: Gather required machinery: chainsaws, excavator, large sieves, and a field spring balance.

Cattle scale: place a flat piece of plywood on the levelled load beams, set car tyres on the plywood to cushion samples, power the monitor with a 12 V car battery; capacity 2000 kg, precision 0.2 kg. Use this fixed‑plate scale to weigh rootballs (samples are moved to the scale).

Digital crane scale: attach to a Hiab crane on a vehicle; capacity 500 kg, precision 0.02 kg. Lift samples in a cargo net or tared lifting straps to weigh stems, large and small branches, foliage, smaller rootballs, and small roots.
Digital balance: place on a level tabletop; capacity 10 kg, precision 0.005 kg. Protect it from wind and sunlight by housing it in a tent; use for weighing sub‑samples of tree components.

Laboratory balances: set two balances on a laboratory tabletop – one 10 kg balance (precision 0.1 g) for dry‑weight samples and one 40 kg balance (precision 0.1 g) for wood‑density measurements. Calibrate both balances before use.
